variations: Easy or spectator version for a puppy or cautious dog: two shallow trays with towels only, one find just under a single fold, a couple of minutes with you close by.
Senior, low-mobility or seated-owner version: low trays on a rug so there is no stepping or crouching, every find in the top layer, and the whole survey run from a chair.
Return visit: a week later, set up the same four trenches with the fills swapped and see whether the Prime Site changes.

Permit version (own yard): stake a hand-lettered permit sign by one legal pit of loose soil or sand, free of glass and sprays, and bury a toy too big to swallow there. The pit is the only place that pays. Stop if they eat soil.
substitutes: A laundry basket or a plastic storage bin instead of a box
A dish towel or a T-shirt instead of a hand towel
title: The Canine Archaeologist
clue: Something familiar lies under the layers, and the survey team is very good at ignoring instructions.
reveal: Open a dig site with four trenches: four shallow trays, four different safe fills and a find or two among them. Your dog chooses where to excavate and for how long, and you chart the survey on a site map.
objective: Offer four trays with different safe fills, let your dog choose where to dig, and chart what they excavated first on a site map.
instructions: Gather four shallow trays or boxes of similar size (baking trays, a low box, a laundry basket lid). Fill each with something different and safe: rolled towels, loosely crumpled plain paper, fabric scraps bigger than a fist, or dry leaves raked from your own yard with conkers, acorns, mushrooms and glass picked out. Nothing taped, tied or small enough to swallow.

Choose two of your dog's own toys, too big to swallow. Tuck one just under the top layer of one trench and the other deeper in a second trench. Leave two trenches with nothing at all, the 'sterile ground'. Mark the trays A to D with scraps of card.

Draw the site map: a rectangle on paper with four boxes in the same order as the trays, labeled A to D. Set the trays in a row on a non-slip floor with room between them, sit down nearby, say 'the survey is open' once and wait. Do not point or hold things out.
Watch which trench your dog visits first, where they dig and where they linger. Number each visit on the map in order (1, 2, 3) with a word or two: 'nosed', 'dug', 'left'. Their route is the survey.

Watch for frustration, such as whining, stopping or frantic pawing. Quietly lift a layer away to make it easier. If paper or fabric starts being chewed or swallowed, calmly lift it out and swap that fill for a towel. Whatever they find is theirs; no tug, no taking it back.
Close the dig when your dog loses interest, has seen all four trenches, or after about fifteen minutes. Put water down and leave the site alone for a quiet rest.

Write the Site Report. The trench they chose first is the Prime Site; the one they worked longest is the Richest Layer, even if it was empty. Set the finds on a low shelf with a scrap of card beside each for a few days, then return them to the toy basket.
twist: The dig is a choice, not a contest: four grounds, finds in only two of them, and a site map that records which trench your dog trusted first.
completion: Your dog has visited the trenches in their own way, the site map has its numbers and the finds are on display.
photoIdea: Your dog's nose or paw in the dig site, shot from the side at their level, or the finished museum shelf with the labels.
memoryPrompt: Which trench did your dog choose first, and what did they find there?
supplies: Fills: towels, plain paper, fabric scraps or dry leaves
Two of your dog's own toys, too large to swallow
safety: Use plain uncolored paper and towels, and lift out any paper or fabric your dog chews or swallows.
Make finds too big to swallow. Puppies: towel fills only, no crumpled paper, a couple of minutes at most.
Leaves: only your own dry, freshly raked leaves, with conkers, acorns, mushrooms and glass picked out.
